---
title: Kettle Row composting pilot, six-month report
type: source
---

The Brayling Public Works Department ran a curbside food waste collection pilot in the
Kettle Row district from March 2 to September 1, 2026. The town council authorized the
pilot in November 2025, after an RFP for hauling drew three bids and the lowest of them
came in under the estimate the department had published.

The department invited 640 households and enrolled 412, a sign-up rate of 64 percent.
Each enrolled household received a sealed cart and a countertop pail. Collection ran every
Wednesday. Loads went to the Sorrel Street transfer station and from there to a windrow
site outside the town limits.

Over the six months the pilot diverted 63 tons of food waste from the landfill. At the
county tipping fee of 38 dollars per ton, that diversion avoided 2,394 dollars in disposal
charges. The pilot cost 15,244 dollars to run over the same six months, a figure covering
the carts, the pails, the hauling contract, and a quarter of the coordinator's salary.
Marta Vinh, the pilot coordinator, writes that the per household cost of 74 dollars per
year is the figure a full rollout would have to carry, and that it does not fall much as
volume rises.

Participation was measured as the share of enrolled households setting a cart out in a
given week. It averaged 68 percent across the pilot. In July it fell to 51 percent. The
report attributes the July drop to odor. The department logged 37 odor complaints over the
pilot, and 29 of those came in July.

Contamination was measured by hand sorting one load a month. Plastic bags, coffee cup lids
and produce stickers made up 11 percent of the first month's sampled load by weight. By the
sixth month that share was 4 percent. Vinh credits a second mailer and a set of stickers
printed for the cart lids.

Total MSW tonnage collected from the Kettle Row district fell 12 percent against the same
six months of 2025. The report notes that the diverted food waste accounts for most, though
not all, of that decline, and that the district also lost 18 households to vacancy over the
stretch.

Ellis Trant, the public works director, recommends extending the pilot for a second six
months rather than expanding it. The recommendation rests on the cost gap: the avoided
disposal charges cover a small fraction of what the program costs to run. Trant argues the
case for the program has to be made on the 12 percent tonnage figure and on the windrow
site's compost yield rather than on the tipping fee alone.

The report leaves two questions open. It does not estimate what a townwide program would
cost, and it does not say whether the windrow site can take the volume a townwide program
would produce. The council is scheduled to take the recommendation up in October.
